blocks.text: A routine blood film from a feverish child shows crowds of cells with segmented nuclei, while a film from a child with a viral illness shows many small round-nucleus cells instead. Reading a film means recognising each formed element by size, nucleus and cytoplasm, and knowing which marrow lineage it came from.

blocks.markdown: Blood is a specialised connective tissue. Its cellular fraction consists of **formed elements** suspended in plasma: erythrocytes carry oxygen, platelets take part in haemostasis, and leucocytes provide immune defence. On a film stained with a Romanowsky stain (Wright or Giemsa), acidic structures take up the blue dye and basic structures such as haemoglobin and eosinophil granules take up the red dye.

blocks.title: Haemopoiesis
blocks.text: Haemopoiesis is the production of blood cells from haemopoietic stem cells, which after birth live mainly in red bone marrow. A haemopoietic stem cell is a self-renewing precursor that can give rise to every blood cell lineage.

blocks.caption: Myeloid branch of haemopoiesis (HSC = haemopoietic stem cell)

blocks.latex: \text{HSC} \rightarrow \text{common lymphoid progenitor} \rightarrow \begin{cases}\text{B lymphocytes}\\ \text{T lymphocytes}\\ \text{natural killer cells}\end{cases}
blocks.caption: Lymphoid branch of haemopoiesis

blocks.title: Identifying cells on a blood film
blocks.prompt: A film shows many pink anucleate biconcave discs, one cell slightly larger than the discs with a multilobed nucleus and pale pink-lilac cytoplasm, and a tiny purple fragment with no nucleus. Identify each structure.

steps.text: The pink anucleate biconcave discs with central pallor are erythrocytes (about 7-8 micrometres across). Absence of a nucleus and uniform size are the key clues.

The cell only slightly larger than an erythrocyte (about 10-12 micrometres) with a nucleus in 2-5 connected lobes and pale fine granules is a neutrophil, the most abundant circulating leucocyte in healthy adults. It is not the largest leucocyte; that is the monocyte.
The tiny purple fragment (about 2-3 micrometres) without a nucleus is a platelet, a cytoplasmic fragment shed from a marrow megakaryocyte.

rows: Pale pink-lilac with fine specific granules
Round, dense, fills most of the cell
Thin rim of sky-blue cytoplasm, no specific granules
blocks.caption: The formed elements of a peripheral blood film

blocks.markdown: The **myeloid lineage** gives erythrocytes, platelets, the three **granulocytes** (neutrophil, eosinophil, basophil) and monocytes. The **lymphoid lineage** gives B lymphocytes, T lymphocytes and natural killer cells. Monocytes circulate for a short time, then enter tissues and mature into macrophages.

Two quantitative skills follow from this. First, the **absolute count** of any cell type equals the total white cell count multiplied by its fraction in the differential: $\text{absolute count} = \text{WBC} \times \text{fraction}$, usually reported in $10^9$ cells per litre. A percentage alone can mislead when the total is abnormal. Second, erythrocytes act as an **internal ruler** on a film: because they are close to 7.5 micrometres, a cell's true size is its apparent size multiplied by $7.5 / (\text{apparent erythrocyte size})$.

blocks.title: Tracing a progenitor to mature blood cells
blocks.prompt: A marrow precursor is committed to the common lymphoid progenitor. Which mature blood cells can it generate?

steps.text: Identify the progenitor class: the common lymphoid progenitor belongs to the lymphoid lineage.
From the lineage map, lymphoid progenitors generate B lymphocytes, T lymphocytes and natural killer cells.
So erythrocytes, platelets, granulocytes and monocytes are not expected descendants; they come from the myeloid branch.

blocks.answer: B lymphocytes, T lymphocytes and natural killer cells.

items: Decide first whether the cell is an erythrocyte, a platelet or a leucocyte, and check for a nucleus.
For a leucocyte, judge size and nuclear shape: segmented, round and dense, indented, or obscured.
Then look at the cytoplasm: pale with fine granules, sky-blue and scant, grey-blue and abundant, red-orange granules, or blue-purple granules.

blocks.title: Do not confuse neutrophils with lymphocytes
blocks.text: A neutrophil is slightly larger than an erythrocyte and has a segmented nucleus with pale cytoplasm and fine granules. A small lymphocyte is about the size of an erythrocyte or a little larger, with a round dense nucleus filling most of the cell and only a thin rim of cytoplasm. Nuclear shape is usually the fastest discriminator.

points: Erythrocytes and platelets are anucleate; leucocytes are nucleated and comprise neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, lymphocytes and monocytes, distinguished by size, nuclear shape and cytoplasm.
Haemopoietic stem cells in marrow self-renew and give a common myeloid progenitor (erythrocytes, platelets, granulocytes, monocytes) and a common lymphoid progenitor (B, T and natural killer cells).
Absolute counts are total white cell count times differential fraction, and erythrocytes serve as an internal size ruler on a film.

questions.stem: A film from a patient with hay fever shows a cell a little larger than the surrounding erythrocytes, with a bilobed nucleus and numerous coarse red-orange granules. Which cell is this?

options.text: Eosinophil
Basophil
Neutrophil
Monocyte

distractorRationale.a: Correct: bilobed nucleus with coarse red-orange granules is an eosinophil.
distractorRationale.b: Basophil granules are deep blue-purple and obscure the nucleus.
distractorRationale.c: Neutrophils have 2-5 lobes and pale fine granules.
distractorRationale.d: Monocytes have a kidney-shaped nucleus and grey-blue cytoplasm without coarse granules.

questions.explanation: Eosinophil granules bind the acidic red dye, giving the red-orange colour, and the nucleus is typically bilobed. Allergic disease is one setting where eosinophils are prominent.

questions.stem: Between the cells on a film are small clusters of purple-granular fragments, 2-3 micrometres across, with no nucleus. From which marrow cell do these structures arise?

options.text: Fragmentation of the cytoplasm of a megakaryocyte
Extrusion of the nucleus from an erythroblast
Budding from a monocyte
Division of a mature lymphocyte

questions.correctOptionText: Fragmentation of the cytoplasm of a megakaryocyte

distractorRationale.a: Correct: platelets are shed from megakaryocyte cytoplasm.
distractorRationale.b: Nuclear extrusion produces a reticulocyte, which is an erythrocyte precursor, not a platelet.
distractorRationale.d: Lymphocytes divide as whole cells and are nucleated.

questions.explanation: Platelets are anucleate cytoplasmic fragments, so they cannot arise by cell division. They are shed from megakaryocytes, which sit in the myeloid branch of haemopoiesis.

questions.stem: A genetic defect prevents formation of the common lymphoid progenitor but leaves the rest of haemopoiesis intact. Which cell count would you expect to remain normal?

options.text: Neutrophils
B lymphocytes
T lymphocytes
Natural killer cells

distractorRationale.a: Correct: neutrophils derive from the myeloid branch.
distractorRationale.b: B cells derive from the lymphoid progenitor.
distractorRationale.c: T cell precursors derive from the lymphoid progenitor.
distractorRationale.d: Natural killer cells are lymphoid derivatives.

questions.explanation: Neutrophils are granulocytes and come from the common myeloid progenitor, so they are unaffected when the lymphoid branch is blocked. B cells, T cells and natural killer cells all depend on the lymphoid progenitor.

questions.stem: A patient has a total white cell count of 6.0 x 10^9 cells per litre. The differential reports 30% lymphocytes. Calculate the absolute lymphocyte count in units of 10^9 cells per litre.
questions.explanation: Absolute count equals total white cell count multiplied by the fraction: 6.0 x 0.30 = 1.8 x 10^9 per litre. Reporting absolute counts avoids the misleading effect a percentage can have when the total count is abnormal.

questions.stem: Outline the differentiation of a haemopoietic stem cell into myeloid and lymphoid lineages in adult marrow.
markingGuide: Haemopoietic stem cells reside in red bone marrow and are self-renewing.
They commit to a common myeloid progenitor or a common lymphoid progenitor.
Myeloid lineage gives erythrocytes, megakaryocytes/platelets, granulocytes (neutrophil, eosinophil, basophil) and monocytes.
Lymphoid lineage gives B lymphocytes, T lymphocytes and natural killer cells.
Does not place cells in the wrong lineage.
questions.explanation: A good answer presents a branching scheme with a self-renewing stem cell at the root. Marks depend on placing each mature cell on the correct branch.

questions.stem: A cell on a film measures about twice an erythrocyte's diameter. It has an indented, kidney-shaped nucleus with fine lacy chromatin and abundant grey-blue cytoplasm containing a few vacuoles. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It is a monocyte, a myeloid-lineage cell that can become a tissue macrophage
It is a large lymphocyte, a lymphoid-lineage cell
It is a neutrophil, recognised by its segmented nucleus
It is a basophil, recognised by its blue-purple granules

questions.correctOptionText: It is a monocyte, a myeloid-lineage cell that can become a tissue macrophage

distractorRationale.a: Correct on identity, lineage and fate.
distractorRationale.b: A lymphocyte has a round dense nucleus and scant cytoplasm.
distractorRationale.c: Neutrophils have a segmented nucleus and are smaller.
distractorRationale.d: Basophils have coarse blue-purple granules that obscure the nucleus.

questions.explanation: The large size, indented nucleus with lacy chromatin and abundant grey-blue cytoplasm identify a monocyte, the largest normal leucocyte. It arises from the myeloid branch and enters tissues to mature into a macrophage.

questions.stem: On a projected image, an erythrocyte measures 9 mm across and a neutrophil measures 14 mm. Taking the true erythrocyte diameter as 7.5 micrometres, calculate the true neutrophil diameter in micrometres.
questions.explanation: The erythrocyte gives the scale: 7.5 micrometres / 9 mm. The neutrophil is 14 x 7.5 / 9 = 11.7 micrometres, which fits the expected 10-12 micrometres and shows a neutrophil is only slightly larger than an erythrocyte.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'A lymphocyte has a segmented nucleus and fine pale granules, while a neutrophil has a round dense nucleus and a thin rim of cytoplasm.' Explain why this is incorrect and give the correct description of each cell.
markingGuide: The features of neutrophil and lymphocyte have been swapped.
Neutrophil: multilobed nucleus (2-5 lobes), pale cytoplasm with fine granules, 10-12 micrometres.
Lymphocyte: round dense nucleus filling most of the cell, thin rim of cytoplasm, no specific granules, smaller.
Identifies nuclear shape as the key discriminator.
questions.explanation: The student has reversed the two descriptions. A strong answer restates each cell correctly, stressing nuclear shape and cytoplasm amount.

questions.stem: Which statement about monocytes is correct?

options.text: They arise from the myeloid branch and mature into macrophages after entering tissues
They arise from the common lymphoid progenitor and become plasma cells
They are anucleate fragments shed from megakaryocytes
They are granulocytes with a segmented nucleus

questions.correctOptionText: They arise from the myeloid branch and mature into macrophages after entering tissues

distractorRationale.b: Monocytes are myeloid, not lymphoid; plasma cells derive from B cells.
distractorRationale.d: Monocytes have an indented nucleus and are not classed as granulocytes.

questions.explanation: Monocytes are myeloid-lineage cells that circulate briefly and then migrate into tissues, where they differentiate into macrophages. They are neither lymphoid cells nor fragments, and they are not granulocytes.

questions.stem: You are given a film containing a cell with a nucleus almost obscured by coarse deep blue-purple granules and another with a bilobed nucleus and coarse red-orange granules. Explain how you would identify each and why both are classed as granulocytes, contrasting them with a lymphocyte.
markingGuide: Blue-purple granules obscuring a lobed nucleus: basophil.
Bilobed nucleus with red-orange granules: eosinophil.
Both are granulocytes because they carry prominent specific granules and derive from the myeloid branch.
Lymphocyte has a round dense nucleus, scant sky-blue cytoplasm, no specific granules, and is lymphoid in origin.
questions.explanation: Granule colour on a Romanowsky stain separates eosinophils from basophils. Both share the granulocyte category with the neutrophil, whereas the lymphocyte lacks specific granules and arises from the lymphoid lineage.
